To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the diagnosis and treatment of osteoporosis in patients who present to the orthopaedic office with a fragility-related fracture is suboptimal, (b) the orthopaedists who treat these patients are uncertain about their responsibilities in this area, and (c) the orthopaedic community is receptive to the notion of assuming greater responsibility for diagnosis and treatment of these patients.

1) Orthopaedic surgeons are in an excellent position to initiate osteoporosis treatment in patients with fragility fractures; 2) Most patients with fragility fracture do not receive osteoporosis therapy; 3) Barriers to osteoporosis therapy exist; and 4) The orthopaedic community is beginning to take a more proactive role in addressing this issue.

1) most patients who present with fragility fractures are not evaluated or treated by any physician for osteoporosis, and 2) orthopaedic surgeons have a key opportunity to initiate definitive evaluation and treatment of osteoporosis in their fragility fracture patients, as supported by recent guidelines.
